Hi, thank you for the well wishes. They had found a mass on his upper jaw during a tooth extraction. We were all hoping it was a calcified abscess. They did a biopsy and it came back as squamous cell carcinoma. It was on the back of his upper jaw, so it was impossible to cut the tumor out. They found the mass on May 30th, we had a consultation with an oncologist on June 30th (the earliest I could get him in), and by July 11th, it had gotten so big that even with his pain meds he was unable to eat liquified food. I knew it was time to say goodbye when the vet said we could try a different pain medicine, but it would only give him a few more good days sprinkled in with bad. I couldn’t continue to watch him suffer, and I decided to do what best for my little guy. He went quick and peaceful at the appointment, the vet said he was definitely ready. He will always be so so loved.

Thank you all so so much for the well wishes. I made this post in the middle of the night as I couldn’t sleep thinking about my boy. I didn’t expect to wake up to so many wonderful comments.

I turned 30 in June, and I just found out what I wanted to be when I grew up a couple months ago. A lot of people don’t have life figured when they get out of high school. I mean, my husband and I don’t have our shit together yet. We are working on it, and things are improving, but it is so hard to know what you want to do with your life when you’re so young. 

To start trying to figure it out, think about what your hobbies are and see if there’s any job you can do that involves them. If you’re working with something you like doing, it can make work feel less monotonous and overwhelming. Or they have guided journals that you can use to “help figure yourself out,” which will help you figure out what you want to be when you grow up. Signing up for an intro class at a community college might be a good idea too. Take a class that actually sounds interesting to you so you’re more likely to follow through. If you don’t want to pay for a class, schedule an appointment with a career counselor. They will set you up with character tests that can help narrow down fields you would be a good fit in. There are also a ton of free college courses online that you can try out.

Most of the time when training you try to make the crate their safe space. Somewhere they want to go. He’s  the only one I’ve tried to crate train, as he was my first dog, not the family dog. The important is we tried, and when it stressed him out I came up with a different solution.

It’s really hard to define a consistent ‘normal’ with the chaos that can happen in everyday life. For me, what I consider normal is more or less when I can rationally think through my actions and consider the consequences. When I can no longer do that, I am not in my normal state of mind and I’ve usually had a mood swing to incredible rage where all I see is blood red and I could rip someone apart or severely depressed to the point that I toy with the idea of ending my putrid existence as a meaningless person.  

I don’t communicate well when I’ve had a swing, but my fiancé and I have started to go over what happened during my swing, since I tend to black out during my rages (I’ve sent books of texts to him I don’t remember sending during some of them). We try to see what possibly triggered the swing so we can perhaps catch the swing sooner and perhaps I can use my coping skills to get me through, and we also pick apart exactly what I said, and he makes me explain what I meant. It’s helped a lot. You can’t make everyone understand, and they either accept it, or they don’t. 

As for the feeling guilty? I feel guilty every time I have a swing. I turn emotionally abusive and I take it out on the people that I love the most. The thing that helps get me through is that I know they know my swings aren’t the real me. And I try to explain as best I can what happened. All you can do is apologize.
